title: Why costly crude oil moves your Nifty
intro: Why can a fight in a faraway sea make petrol, vegetables and the Nifty costlier on the same day? Four steps.
steps: India imports most of its crude
We pay for it in dollars. There is no local tap to open.
The price jumps
A costlier barrel raises India's import bill overnight.
Fuel and transport get costlier
Trucks, flights and factories burn fuel, so everyday prices follow.
Profits squeeze, stocks wobble
Companies spend more and earn less, and the Nifty feels it.
oneline: When you read “crude up”, read: India's costs went up today.

title: What is India VIX?
intro: Markets have a fear meter. It is called India VIX. Here is how to read it.
steps: It measures expected swings
VIX shows how much the market expects Nifty to move over the next 30 days.
High VIX means nervous
Big expected swings mean investors are worried or unsure.
Low VIX means calm
Small expected swings mean the market feels comfortable.
It is not a prediction
It shows the mood, not the direction. It can be high on up days too.
oneline: VIX up means fear up. It tells you the mood, not where the market goes.

title: Why bank stocks fall first on red days
intro: On a red day, bank stocks often fall faster than others. Why?
steps: Banks touch everything
Loans, savings and businesses all run through banks, so they feel every worry first.
Big investors own them most
Banks are heavily owned by large funds, which sell fast when nervous.
Rates and bad loans matter
Rising rates and loan defaults hit bank profits directly.
They also rise fast
The same size makes them bounce quickly when mood improves.
oneline: Banks are the market's mirror: they show the mood first.

title: What is the rupee, and why does it move?
intro: The rupee goes up and down against the dollar every day. Here is why.
steps: It is a price
USD/INR is the price of one dollar in rupees.
Dollars in, rupee up
When foreign money flows into India, more buyers want rupees.
Dollars out, rupee down
Costly oil or foreign selling means more demand for dollars.
Why you care
A weaker rupee makes imports, travel and foreign education costlier.
oneline: More dollars coming in means a stronger rupee.

title: Sensex vs Nifty: what is the difference?
intro: Two numbers, one story. What are they?
steps: Both are baskets
Each index tracks a group of big companies to show how the market did.
Sensex has 30
The BSE's index of 30 large companies.
Nifty has 50
The NSE's index of 50 large companies.
They move together
They are mostly similar, so one tells you the other's story.
oneline: Sensex and Nifty are two scorecards for the same big companies.

title: Why does the market open at 9:15?
intro: Trading does not start the moment you wake up. India's market has a fixed daily rhythm.
steps: 9:00 to 9:15 is pre-open
Orders are collected and a fair opening price is worked out.
9:15 is the opening bell
Normal buying and selling starts at the price found in pre-open.
Trading runs to 3:30 PM
The close is the last price of the day. That is the number we record.
Weekends and holidays are closed
No trading, so no new closing price.
oneline: Pre-open finds the price, 9:15 opens trading, 3:30 PM sets the close.

title: Who are FIIs and DIIs?
intro: You often hear that foreigners sold and Indian funds bought. Who are they?
steps: FII means foreign institutional investor
Large overseas funds that invest in Indian shares.
DII means domestic institutional investor
Indian mutual funds, insurers and similar large investors.
Their flows are published daily
Exchanges report how much each group bought and sold.
Flows are information, not instructions
They show what big money did, not what you should do.
oneline: FIIs are foreign funds, DIIs are Indian funds, and their daily buying and selling is public data.

title: What is the repo rate?
intro: The RBI has one rate that quietly touches loans, deposits and markets.
steps: Banks borrow from the RBI
The repo rate is the rate they pay for that short-term money.
It sets the tone for lending rates
When it changes, home and car loan rates often follow.
It affects deposits too
Banks adjust what they pay savers.
Markets read it as a signal
Rate-sensitive sectors like banks and housing watch it closely.
oneline: The repo rate is the RBI's lending rate to banks, and it ripples into loans, deposits and markets.

title: What is inflation (CPI)?
intro: Why does the same ₹100 buy less than it did a few years ago?
steps: Prices of a basket are tracked
CPI follows what households typically buy: food, fuel, housing and more.
The change over a year is inflation
If the basket cost 5% more, inflation is 5%.
Food moves it the most
Vegetables and grains carry a large weight in India's basket.
The RBI keeps an eye on it
Its rate decisions are linked to the inflation reading.
oneline: Inflation is how much more the same basket of goods costs than a year ago.

title: What is the P/E ratio?
intro: One number that says how much you pay for each rupee of a company's profit.
steps: Price is the share price
What one share costs today.
Earnings is profit per share
Called EPS, from the latest results.
Divide price by earnings
A P/E of 20 means ₹20 paid for every ₹1 of yearly profit.
Compare with similar companies
A P/E means little alone. Compare within the same sector.
oneline: P/E is the price paid for each rupee of profit, and it is best compared within a sector.

title: What is market cap?
intro: Market cap tells you how big a company is, not how expensive its share is.
steps: Multiply price by shares
Share price times the total number of shares.
It is the market's value of the company
Not the money the company holds.
Sizes get labels
SEBI ranks the top 100 as large cap, the next 150 as mid cap, the rest as small cap.
Size changes the kind of risk
Small caps usually swing more than large caps.
oneline: Market cap is share price times number of shares: the size of a company.

title: What is a SIP?
intro: Investing a fixed amount on a fixed date, instead of one big lump sum.
steps: You pick an amount and a date
For example ₹1,000 on the 5th of each month.
The money goes into a mutual fund
Automatically, with no need to time the market.
You buy more units when prices are low
And fewer when prices are high.
Time does the heavy lifting
The habit matters more than the exact amount.
oneline: A SIP is a fixed amount invested regularly, so you do not have to pick the right day.

title: What is NAV?
intro: Every mutual fund unit has a price. It is called NAV.
steps: The fund owns many shares
Its total value is the value of everything it holds.
Costs are taken out
Then the rest is divided by the number of units.
That gives NAV per unit
Calculated once a day after the market closes.
Low NAV does not mean cheap
A ₹20 NAV fund is not better than a ₹200 NAV fund.
oneline: NAV is the value of one fund unit, worked out after each day's close.

title: What happens in an IPO?
intro: The first time a company offers its shares to the public.
steps: A private company decides to list
It wants money from many investors.
A price band is announced
Investors bid for shares within that range.
Allotment follows
If more people apply than shares exist, shares are allotted by lottery.
Shares start trading
The company then has a market price every day.
oneline: An IPO is a company's first public share sale, after which its shares trade daily.

title: What is a dividend?
intro: Some companies share part of their profit with shareholders.
steps: The company earns a profit
It can keep it or pay some out.
The board declares a dividend
A rupee amount per share.
Eligible holders are paid
Those holding shares on the record date.
Share price adjusts
It usually drops by about the dividend on the ex-date.
oneline: A dividend is a share of profit paid to shareholders, not a free bonus.

title: Why do bond prices fall when yields rise?
intro: It sounds backwards at first. It is just fair pricing.
steps: An old bond pays a fixed interest
Say 7% on its face value.
New bonds start paying more
If new ones offer 8%, the old one looks worse.
The old bond's price must fall
So that buying it gives a similar return.
That is why yield and price move opposite
Prices down, yield up, and the reverse.
oneline: When new bonds pay more, old bonds must get cheaper, so price and yield move opposite ways.

title: What is a circuit breaker?
intro: A pause button for the market on very wild days.
steps: Single stocks have price bands
A stock can only move a set percentage in a day.
Index circuit breakers exist too
If the Nifty or Sensex falls 10%, 15% or 20%, trading halts.
The pause cools things down
It gives everyone time to read the news.
It is rare
Most days never come close.
oneline: Circuit breakers stop trading for a while when prices move too far, too fast.

title: What is diversification?
intro: Not keeping all your eggs in one basket, in plain terms.
steps: One company can go wrong
Bad news hits one stock harder than the whole market.
Spread across sectors
Banks, IT, pharma, FMCG react differently to the same news.
Spread across asset types
Shares, bonds, gold and cash behave differently.
It reduces surprise, not risk to zero
The whole market can still fall.
oneline: Diversification spreads money so one bad event hurts less.

title: What is compounding?
intro: Earning returns on your earlier returns.
steps: You invest ₹1,000 at 10% a year
After year one you have ₹1,100.
Year two earns on ₹1,100
Not on the original ₹1,000, so you gain ₹110.
Growth speeds up
Each year's base is bigger than the last.
Time matters most
Starting earlier beats investing more later.
oneline: Compounding is growth on top of earlier growth, and it needs time.

title: What is EPS?
intro: Profit per share, the number under the P/E ratio.
steps: Take the company's profit
After tax, from the results.
Divide by the number of shares
That gives profit per share.
Track it quarter by quarter
Rising EPS means profit per share is growing.
Check why it changed
Higher profit, or fewer shares? The reason matters.
oneline: EPS is a company's profit divided by its number of shares.
